metadata.title: Measuring digital literacy across three age cohorts: Exploring test dimensionality and performance differences

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected primary and secondary school student data in Hong Kong (Primary 3, Secondary 1, Secondary 3) using a school-based sampling of 18 primary and 14 secondary schools. The paper reports raw cohort sample sizes and uses IRT-based scoring (2PLM/M2PLM) and subsequent ANOVA/DIF procedures, but it does not report the use of any complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight schemes. Because the analysis is based on a locally administered assessment with a fixed school sample and the manuscript does not describe population-representative weighting, no explicit weight variable is provided. Analysts should therefore treat the results as descriptive/inferential within the sampled Hong Kong schools rather than as nationally weighted estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use ILSA-style Plausible Values (PV) for cognitive achievement. Instead, it estimates latent digital literacy ability using an IRT two-parameter logistic model (2PLM) and reports EAP reliability and DIF screening, so PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not provide a documented missing-data strategy for item non-response beyond noting that gender analyses have smaller sample sizes due to item non-response, so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study used a cross-cohort panel design with one wave conducted in 2018/2019 in Hong Kong. Schools were sampled from four district areas: 18 primary schools and 14 secondary schools participated. Students completed the DL test on desktop/laptop/tablet and could choose English or Chinese; responses from 57 students who took the Chinese version but indicated they speak English at home were discarded because their raw scores were significantly lower, suggesting comprehension difficulties. The final analytic sample for overall DL scores is N=1,989 (Primary 3: 715; Secondary 1: 705; Secondary 3: 569), and gender analyses use smaller Ns due to item non-response.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This paper develops and validates a performance-based digital literacy (DL) assessment aligned to DigComp 2.1 and administers it to Hong Kong students in three cohorts (Primary 3, Secondary 1, Secondary 3) in 2018/2019. The assessment uses 80 items across three test forms (45/50/50 items) with constrained response formats (multiple-choice variants, drop-down, drag-and-drop, short response, and click-image). Psychometric analyses fit unidimensional and multidimensional IRT models (2PLM vs M2PLM), finding that DL is essentially unidimensional: AIC/BIC favored 2PLM over M2PLM and latent correlations among the five modeled competences were high (0.83–0.95). After item purification (discarding low-discrimination items and one gender DIF item), the final 73-item pool produced good measurement quality (RMSD 0.007–0.077; EAP reliability ~0.84–0.86). Performance differences were significant across cohorts (ANOVA F(2,1986)=592.43, p<.001, η2=0.374) and gender effects emerged only in secondary cohorts (gender main effect F(1,1961)=20.93, p<.001, η2=0.011; gender×cohort interaction F(2,1961)=4.86, p<.01, η2=0.005). Limitations include the absence of a documented missing-data handling protocol and the fact that the study is psychometric/measurement-focused rather than ML predictive modeling. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an empirical assessment-development and psychometric validation study using IRT (2PLM/M2PLM), DIF screening, and ANOVA to compare cohort and gender differences. It does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models, and it does not use PV-based achievement outcomes; therefore ml_techniques and main_findings for ML targets are intentionally empty. The manuscript also does not report a formal missing-data handling method beyond noting item non-response reduces Ns for gender analyses, which is why missing_data_handling is set to not_reported.
